Rev. Mr. Bunchel preaches on the stature
of Christ's Stature.


Rev. N. A. Bunchel preached an interest-
ing sermon yesterday morning, to a good
audience, at the Central-avenue Methodist
Church. His text was follows:


Till we all attain unto the unity of the faith
and of the knowledge of the Son of God unto a
full grown man, unto the measure of the stature
of the fulness of Christ—Eph. iv, 13.


The following is an excerpt from the
sermon:


The letter to the Ephesians is sometimes
called a catholic epistle, for the reason
that it did not spring out of special condi-
tions which called for specific teachings.
The apostle had always before his mind
here a large and dignified programme. He
directs attention to the foundation, the
work and the aim of the church. This
three-fold division is held clearly in view
in every part of this letter. In the para-
graph from which this text is taken it is
evident that the apostle is considering the
aim or purpose he had in view in the organiza-
tion of the church. That is, first, to bring
men to the unity of the faith and knowl-
edge of the Son of God, and, second, to
bring men to a condition of full growth;
the measure of Christ's stature.


There is a religion for children and for
the feeble-minded. It has no requirements
at all. There is also a religion for the
poorly instructed—for the unhappy mil-
lions who have always been in the majority
in this world. It has few requirements.
The Judge of all the earth will do right.
He will know those who would have exhib-
ited St. John's character if they had had
St. John's opportunities.


Then there is also a religion for men and
women who have had their life in the midst
of the light of Christian civilization. This
has two requirements in harmony with the
two purposes for which the church is organ-
ized.


The first of these purposes of the gospel
for men and women is to bring them to a
condition of unity of faith and of knowl-
edge of the Son of God. At our first thought
this will appear impossible. We are accus-
tomed to remind ourselves that men are
unlike in their mental constitution even as
they are unlike in their physical aspect.
And from this diversity we hastily conclude
that there are no points of unity among
men. But when we look more carefully
into human nature we find marks of like-
ness which are as striking as the diversity
which we have noted. The soul of man in
its normal condition shows certain strong
and universal characteristics, such as the
capacity for friendship and the hunger for
love. In nothing is this unity of human
nature more surprisingly exhibited than in
the manner in which men have estimated
Jesus Christ. The Roman Catholics, the
Greek Catholics and all the Protestant
bodies speak practically one language in
making estimate of Jesus Christ. Not only
so, the whole world of sincere and honest
argument concerning Jesus Christ, where there
have been reasonably favorable conditions
to consider the person and the teaching of
Jesus.


The condition of unity of knowledge of
the Son of God follows as a necessary re-
sult of true faith. He walking by faith
brings one very quickly into a large and
delightful place where one walks by sight.
The life of companionship with Jesus
Christ is as intensely real as any fact in the
material world.


The second purpose of the gospel is to
bring men to a certain condition of manly
character, described here the measure of
Christ's stature. The gospel is not a re-
ligion of faith and worship only. The
partial and imperfect religions have these
features in some measure. But Christ's re-
ligion is pre-eminently and exclusively the
religion of character. The ultimate pur-
pose of faith and knowledge is to reach the
grade of full growth in manliness. I must
urge you to fix it clearly in your minds
that this is not merely incidental and sub-
sidiary to some other purpose, but
this is the ulterior purpose of religion.
The church is organized for this. Christian
truth is believed for this. Everything in
the church points to the securing of char-
acter as the final and glorious aim of the
gospel.


Consider how worthy of God is this true
conception of the purpose of the gospel.
It is not to minister to the glory of God in
some indefinite and obscure sense, but in
the improvement of man. Man is the off-
spring of God, and God is pleased with
man and glorified by man only when man sets
his face to the light and makes himself to
become something in character.


The attention of the world is just now
attracted to a most conspicuous illustra-
tion of the manner in which the gospel has
improved man, stimulated him to high
achievements, and quickened him in his
entire being.


In the Midway Plaisance you see illus-
trations of the fact that missionary opera-
tions are necessary. In the World's Fair
you see glorious demonstration of the
fact that missionary operations have sue-
ceeded. In the Midway Plaisance you see
illustrations of the low level of the life of
men who have not been influenced by
Christ's gospel. An hundred years of time
will make practically no difference in the
life of men who are without that intellec-
tual and spiritual stimulus which is the
soul of Christian civilization. In the World's
Fair you see the high level of men who have
been touched by the gospel into the new-
ness of life. An hundred years in the life
of these men shows a tremendous advance-
ment, for the reason that they have ac-
cepted the inspiring gospel which is the
soul of civilization. In the Midway Plai-
sance you see illustrations of the moral
conditions which Jesus Christ found in the
world when He came. In the
World's Fair you see what He has done for
that part of the race that has received the
light of His truth.


If the inspiring source of all this marvel-
ous development should be properly rec-
ognized at the World's Fair one would see
great crosses higher than the Ferris Wheel,
at the north, at the south, at the east and
at the west side of Jackson Park. But
men and women with fine eyes and pure
hearts can see the crosses standing by
every exhibit in all the great buildings,
where anything is shown which relates to
the comfort, the well-being, the improve-
ment and the refinement of man.

THE VICE PRESIDENT'S ROOM.

Interesting Apartment In the Capitol to BE
Occupied by Mr. Stevenson.

The room occupied by A. E. Stevenson as his Office at the Capitol is one of the handsomest as well as one of the most historic in the way of relics there is in the city of Washington, says Washington correspondent of the New York World. In the Senate wing of the Capitol there are two rooms set aside as Offices for the President Of the United States and the Vice President of the United States. The former room is by far the handsomer OF the two, but it is little used as an office. The latter, however, though not as pretty as the President's, is a very beautiful room. It is used daily as the office of the Vice President while the Senate is in session, and it contains some very interesting relics.

It is large and square, with stuccoed ceiling and tinted walls, and is situated just at the end of the Senate lobby. Its furniture consists of a very beautiful ecru-tinted CARPET, five large chairs, including a rocking chair upholstered in dark-green leather, two flat top rosewood tables and an office desk. There is also a large sofa, fire-screen, drop-lights, etc.

The fireplace is one of the old style, wood being used as fuel entirely. Just between the Vice President's seat at the center-table and the fireplace is the large glass screen and this serves to throw off the heat, but still does not spoil the effect OF the burning hickory logs. The large brass fender around the fire used to protect the carpet from the sparks is a very elegant affair, and it has been the custom for many years to give to the retiring Vice President this fender with its accompanying poker, tongs, etc.

In the right-hand corner as you enter the room is a small safe, upon which is marked in gilt letters "Vice President of the United States." This safe is used as repository for the electoral votes as they come from the different States just after election until they are counted in the House of Representatives. The custom prevails, and probably will always prevail, that during the period when the electoral votes are within the safe two officers Of the Capitol police force are detailed to watch them night and day, and they are so vigilant that even the Vice President's Private Secretary is not admitted to the room without one of the officers accompanying him. The combination of the safe is at that time known only to the Vice President then holding the position as President of the Senate.

The former entrance to the Vice President's chamber, just outside of the lobby, has been for some years closed, and the little alcove made thereby is now used as washroom.

This little place contains one of the most interesting relics in the room. It is a small mirror, two and one-half feet long by eighteen inches wide, and was purchased by the Senate for John Adams, the first Vice President Of the United States, who was on the ticket with Washington. It has a very ordinary gilt frame and is made of poor material. Still it caused a great controversy in the Senate at the time of its purchase, some of the Senators objecting TO the price, which was $40, saying that that amount was entirely too much for the government to expend for a mirror, even for the Vice President; but after a lengthy and interesting debate it was decided to buy it. The mirror has received every care and is now almost in perfect condition, having been for the last fifty years in the care of the venerable Capt. Bassett. Another article in the little washroom is a very beautifully carved toilet case. The cabinet is of ebony and was made for Mr. Chester A. Arthur by his special request.

Upon the right wall, looking from the entrance, is a painting of George Washington, considered the best Of Washington in existence. It was executed by Rembrandt Peale in 1875. Peale had three sittings of Washington, and at that time dentistry was not practiced so scientifically as at the present day, and it is a historical fact that at each of these sittings Washington used raw cotton as a substitute for false teeth so as to fill out the mouth and cheeks. This adds great value to the portrait, as it gives his face a determined look, which was very natural in Washington.

Policy OF Retrenchment on this Southern
Pacific.

San Francisco, Cal., Aug. 1.—THE Southern Pacific company in pursuing a policy OF retrenchment has discharged 1,900 employees, decreasing its monthly pay roll not less than $75,600 or at the rate OF $1,000,000 annually. The discharged men were on the Pacific system of lines west of El Paso and Ogden and south of Portland. A reduction has also been made on the Atlantic system east of El Paso, and just to what extent is not known here. The wholesale discharge of employees is indicated by recent reductions of daily hours of labor in the various shops of the system. For some time past nine hours a day has been the rule in these shops, the men being mainly paid by the hour. Now they are working eight hours a day, which is a 10 per cent reduction in time and is said to be equivalent to the discharge of 600 men.

The number of shopmen that have been discharged outright is not less than 300. Dismissals from the force of track men are on a wholesale scale, for not less than 500 of these employees have been discharged. On the Pacific system there are about 1,900 trackmen scattered over California, Oregon, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico and Arizona. The discharges will leave about 1,400 in the states and in the territories named. The force of telegraph operators has also felt the effect, for between ten and twenty of them have been discharged and several train dispatching offices have been abolished. The company has cut down its daily passenger train mileage sufficiently to 100 miles, and has discontinued a number of passenger trains that covered that distance each day. Local freight trains are running about as usual, but every through freight that is sent East or brought West has to be loaded to its full capacity before it is started on its journey. Economy in train service has caused the displacement of about 200 trainmen, including engineers, firemen, brakemen and conductors. The number of trainmen now on the extra or waiting list without pay is said to be over 80, the largest in the history of the company.

Nathan W. Prescott, of the firm of
Prescott & Doran, pawnbrokers at 39½
Wabasha street, was arrested last night
on warrant charging him with having
violated section 305, chapter 10 of the
General Statutes, relating to pawn
brokers. The section which Prescott is
charged with violating reads as follows:
"A pawnbroker who sells any article re-
ceived by him in pledge before the
time for redemption has expired, or
who willfully refuses to disclose the
price taken by him for any article
received by him in pledge and subsequently sold, is
guilty of a misdemeanor."

charge of the pawnbroker records in
the police department, is the one who
swore out the complaint, and he alleges
that Prescott refused to tell him the

name of the purchaser of a watch
which had been pawned and sold before
the time to redeem had expired. Pres-
cott, who was arrested and locked up
for three hours last night before he
could procure bail, says the whole mat-
ter is spite work. In May last he loaned

Minn., but has disposed of the ticket to
another person. The present holder

sired to redeem the watch. There was

take it. Mr. Prescott says the present
owner of the ticket evidently expected
to get $500 watch, and as the article
on which the money was loaned was a
much cheaper one he became sore and
instigated complaint. The case will
come up in the police court this morn-
ing.

in the hard ground at least ten feet
right in the public highway, and the
end which bent over had to be removed
before vehicles could pass.

down and stuck in the ground, varying
in depth, the others falling sideways.

ated in the neighbourhood.

LOWELL, Mass., July 11.— The cry is that times in Lowell are not yet disastrous. There has NOT been a SEASON for many years when there has been greater demand for mechanics than the present one. It is true that two or three of the small machine shops have shut down temporarily for want of orders, and the textile mills (woolen) have begun to run on reduced time, and also that there have been rumors that some of the large corporations would be compelled to suspend operations for a few weeks in order to allow the market to catch up with the new goods demand, but thus far there has been no comparative cessation of the stream of money that is regularly expended for business in this city. The strike of bricklayers has prevented some of the brick work that might have been erected under other circumstances, but at the same time many bricklayers have been obtained from outside the city, and in other cases the union men have had their terms accepted.

At the present time probably more than a quarter of million dollars worth of construction is in progress in this city.

The new post office will be ready to be occupied in about two weeks. The Mass House Mills are engaged in extensive improvement that will largely increase the production of fine goods, it being intended to add 10,000 spindles to the present number this fall and other machinery in proportion, considering the fact that a finer class of goods is to be produced hereafter than has been the case in the past. C. J. Hood & Co. are engaged in doubling the size and capacity of their present large laboratory for the manufacture of sarsaparilla peculiar to itself. A large brewery is in process of erection that will require a million and a half of bricks to be laid and the work must be done this fall. Ex-Mayor Seld is erecting a large machine shop; at least two new business blocks are being erected, and an indefinite number of residences are being erected in all directions.

It is a fact that the mills of this city have run through all blue-sky depressions in the past except during a portion of the war period, when some of them were caught with too large supplies of cotton.

The reason for this is obvious. As shut down cases cause the help to become scattered, no matter if it be only for a couple of weeks, and when the mills start up there is an embarrassment that is unpleasant until a regular supply of employees can be secured. For this reason the mills will run as long as possible before they decide to do anything to curtail production, and as their credit is of the best it is more than possible that with the lifting up of the financial stringency that people will begin to purchase goods they will be enabled to go along without interruption.

The consolidated statement of the national banks of the city also shows remarkably well since May: loans have decreased $105,535; overdrafts have decreased $14,248; surplus and profits have increased $11,373; and deposits have decreased only $119,051. At the present time the surplus and undivided profits of the national banks is $1,155,922, while individual deposits amount to $4,072,240. There is nothing to indicate that the savings banks of the city cannot make an equally good showing.

The Late Mrs. Beach.

ices will be held to morrow, at 2 p. m.

the north and Edgewood avenue on the
south, in reference to the establishment of
building lines, so as to have all the houses
on the streets equally distant from the
roadway. This tract of land used to be
the old town farm.

Among those who expressed themselves
in favor of having uniform building line
were Trustee Burton Mansfield, William
Donnelly, Alderman Macdonald, Eugene
F. Sullivan, Henry S. Daley, J. F. Lyon,
Newton H. Cox, W. R. Harper, Patrick E.
Whelan, John S. Stanley and A. Brazos.
In executive session the committee voted
to recommend the establishment of a
thirty foot line on Edgewood avenue and a
twenty five-foot line on each of the other
streets.

The Late Mrs. Beach.
The death of Mrs. Rebecca G. Beach,
which occurred early yesterday morning,
brings deep and sincere sorrow to many
hearts. The deceased lady had been ill
only a week. She was attacked with a severe form of tonsilitis on her return from
Fishers Island, where she had been
spending a few days, but the symp-
toms were not at first seriously alarming
and her recovery was confidently expect
ed. Later, however, on Sunday the dis
ease assumed a critical form, developing
into capillary bronchitis, and despite the
most devoted and loving care and the eff
orts of the best medical skill she was unable to rally. Her death leaves a void in
the home circle and the circle of near and
dear friends which will ever be deeply
felt. Around her memory the tenderest
thoughts will linger with those who knew
her cultivation of mind and beautiful
traits of disposition and the sweet repose
of her lovely character.

The deceased was native of Whittington, Del., and was the daughter of William
and Rebecca Donaldson Gibbons. Her
husband, the late John S. Beach, to
whom she was married in 1847, was long
one of the leading members of the Con-
necticut bar, a gentleman distinguished
also by his true gentleness and refinement
of character and genuine nobility of ma
ture that made him indeed prince among
men, and in his death the city and state
suffered a distinct loss. The deceased
leaves four children—Rebecca Donaldson
John Kimberly, Frances Gibbons and
Rodman Vernon Beach. The funeral serv-
ices will be held to morrow, at 2 p. m.

Of the many strange ways of bestow-
ing charity which owe their origin to
the eccentric whims of wealthy testa-
tors there are few more peculiar than
that which takes place at the Priory
Church, West Smithfield, every Good
Friday. This is the Money Dole. On
that day twenty-one widows might
have been seen picking up sixpences
from tombstone. This singular Gus
tom has been observed for so many
years that the actual date of its incep-
tion is forgotten. Even the name of
the benefactor is unknown.


1t is stated that sum of money was
originally left by lady to provide
masses each year for the repose of her
soul, but when the Reformation
dawned the trustees were puzzled how
to carry out the bequest without incit-
ing hostile criticism. Eventually they
resolved to distribute the interest
which accrued each year from the
fund to certain number of poor wild
ows, who should be obliged to kneel
over the tomb, and pick up the money
from the stone which covered it. In
this way it was hoped that the recip-
tents would involuntarily offer prayer
for the welfare of her soul.


Another difficulty, however, arose in
the fact that the nave of the churh in
which the lady had been buried had
been demolished, and the site con-
verted into a graveyard. Utterly un-
able to decide where the lady actually
was buried, the trustees selected a
rude, unlettered gravestone in the
churchyard, and upon this slab the
money was placed for the women en-
titled to receive it. About the end of
the last century the fund which sup
ported the charity was diverted, and
since that time the custom has been
maintained by the generous donations
of wealthy people who are unwilling
that such a quaint charity should be
discontinued. The Million.

SAVANNAH, Oct. 13.—Savannah is in the teeth of the storm which at one time threatened to equal in intensity that of Aug. 27, which swept the entire Georgia and South Carolina coast. great amount of pleasure to be obtained
during the time consumed in the ascent
except in taking an occasional rest. At other
times the circumstances require strict at-
tention to business. The summit reached,
however, the view was well worth the slight
inconveniences of the journey. The weather
and atmosphere was very favorable upon
the occasion of this party's visit, and the
view was unfolded in two distinct panor-
amas which were magnificent to the extreme.
From this point view is at once obtained
of almost the entire Willamette valley with
its cities, towns, rivers, groves, grain-fields,
etc., shut in upon the eastern horizon by
the rugged Cascade range from which the
many snow-peaks ascend in increased grand-
eur as the higher points of observation are
obtained. The minor observations through
a field glass are also very interesting. To
the westward there is an intimate succession
of mountains, between whose walls the
meek burntwoodsman dwelleth in happy se-
clusion. But we must yet in elevated
position and pass on over this vast expanse
western confines of the American continent
and beyond to point where the ocean com-
mingles with the sky-blue of heaven. We
hope this will meet the expectations of our
readers so far as the general view is con-
cerned.

take of luncheon, and place ourselves in an
advantageous attitude to witness the sun
sink into the western sea. This was also a
charming scene; but we have no sunset des-
criptions on hand at present, and therefore
will be compelled to omit special mention of
this feature of the programme.

finally to the aborigines who burned their
signal fires on this spot in the misty ages of
the past. The discussion of Indians and
Indian character led to the suggestion of a
social war-dance, which was indulged in and
greatly enjoyed by all present.


There are some of the details of this trip
which are necessarily left out of the account
and the discomforts of sleeping out upon
morning we saw the sun rise. This was
very interesting to some members of the
party who had not before witnessed this
well-known phenomenon of nature. Soon
after the morning meal the descent was be-
gun and was without incident. A little
diversion induced should have been noted
previously, and as the pleasure in mind is
seldom enjoyed here in midsummer it must
not be omitted. At large snow-drifts
one of the ladies of the party undertook
a toboggan slide, and was fairly successful in
so far as she slid although the
absence of necessary conveniences rendered
the act quite hazardous to the sensibilities
not only of the lady herself, but of the en-
tire party.


The vehicles were reached in good season
and after a rest of few hours, the party
started homeward. Six o'clock p. m. found
all safely in their respective homes in Cor-
vallis, somewhat weary and worn, but having
no regrets of the trip to offer.

The dash system of trotting, introduced
for the first time in this country at the
breeders meeting at the Bay District, was
a success. All those who attended the
races appreciated them, but the mistake
of not chasing the horses was made.
Horses who outclassed the others by sew
eral seconds were not handicapped as pro-
posed, and as a consequence the dashes
were lODsided.


This failure to class the horses was
made in many of the heat races, and they
also became so one-sided that they in no
way savOred of racing. Exciting finishes
are what the public wants, and no one
ex ects it to attend race meetings where
they cannot be had. The Paris-mutual
system of betting proved drawback to
the success Of the meeting. In the first
place, the system is bad, but to make it
worse horses, instead of being sold out,
were coupled in field.


In most cases three horses would be sold
out, and the others sold as field Now.
suppose there were three in the field, and
a person thought one would win. He
bought a pool on the field. Now, the
horse he selected won the race. He would
not win what his judgment entitled him

ARTISTS AND ARCHITECTS ORGANIZE FOR THE

PURPOSE.

A meeting of several well-known artists and architects was held in the studio of W. Vanderbilt Allen, No. 50 West Fifty-seventh st., on Tuesday night, at which steps were taken toward the organization of a society to raise the artistic standard of the public buildings of the city and the statues and monuments in the parks and other public places. Richard Hunt was elected president; A. Bell, secretary, and William B. Bigelow, treasurer. Among the many present Thomas W. Wood, J. G. Brown, L. Scott Hartley, William V. Chase, Augustus II. Gardiner, Kenyon Cox, H. Swain, Clifford R. H. Sheffield, W. B. Bigelow, Howard Russell Butler, Elliott Dangerfield, John Rogers, N. J. Hardenberg, W. H. Low, C. O. Carrere, T. S. Dillenboyt, William D. Twombly, Chester Loomis, W. A. Coffin, W. H. Shelton, F. Crowninshield, Herbert Denman, Robert Reid, Irving R. Wiley, F. C. Jones and John La Farge. It was resolved that a meeting be held on April 11, when the organization, to be known the Metropolitan Art Club, will be perfected.

Mr. Allen speaking of the organization, said, "We have not gone into this matter hurriedly or haphazardly; I proposed the idea almost a year ago, since then it has been freely discussed. Prominent amateurs, among whom are Perry Belmont, George W. Vanderbilt and Henry G. Marquand, are interested in the success of the scheme. What we want to do is to put the accessibility and necessity of paintings and wall decoration before the city authorities and a largo. Except for a few decorative paintings in the City Hall, there are almost no paintings in the public buildings in the City of New York. What we propose to do will not cost the City one penny. The Metropolitan Art Club will be open to all. There will be no discrimination whatever. The membership fee will be $3, with $1 a year dues. The money thus raised together with voluntary contributions from members of the club will constitute a fund which will pay for the paintings, statues, and other decorations, in order that we may get the best possible work. A committee will be appointed consisting of three architects, three sculptors and three painters who will have charge of the competitions, which competitions will be annual and the best work will win sometimes, of course. Commission will take the form of orders to known artists or sculptors for certain work; the work finished will then be tendered to the City."

Guaranty Loan Company of Minneapolis
would not open its doors to-day:

"I want to be entirely candid with you.
I do not believe anything can be gained in
the present situation except by a frank
statement of the company's condition.
The company may not be compelled to
close its doors to-morrow, but suspension
cannot be put off more than two or three
days.

"I have been in constant communica-
tion by private wire with President
Menaye for the last three days. I was up
all last night talking to him over this
wire. Some of my financial friends in
New York were with me, and we came to
the conclusion that suspension could not
be averted.

"The company is about ten years old, and
has capital stock of $1,550,600. For several years it has attempted to float com-
mercial paper it took collateral sufficient
to cover the paper and then guaranteed
the payment of the paper.

"All told, it now holds about $4,000,000
of this commercial paper. The stringency
in the money market made it impossible
for our customers to take up or renew
their notes, and unfortunately we cannot
realize on the collateral."

obscure idea of the principle of the
arc and incandescent lamp respec-
lively. In the arc lamp electric
discharge takes place between two
pieces of hard conducting carbon
separated from each other by an
interval which is kept as nearly as
possible constant by automatic de-
vices. An arc or light of intense
brilliance called the voltaic arc is
thus obtained. In the glow or in
candescent lamp a filament of car
bon inclosed in a globe exhausted
of air by a mercury pump serves
as path along which the current
passes. The resistance the cleo
tricity meets with in passing
through this filament is sufficient
to raise the latter to incandes-
cence, and a light is thus obtained
more suitable for the illumination
of interiors generally.

The Free Gold on Hand Monday Expected to Amount to $50,000,000—A Belief That the Golden Tide has Turned in Favor of the Government.

WASHINGTON, March 10.—Secretary Carlisle has received offers from Chicago bankers to exchange $50,900,600 of gold for like amount of small treasury notes of denominations of fives, tens and twenties. Intimations were made that the amount of small notes that will be needed will reach $4,000,000, for which gold will be paid. He will forward the small notes at once. This demand for small notes is explained by the fact that with the opening of spring weather, cattle and grain are beginning to be moved. A slight demand is also being felt farther west, and it is anticipated that the demand for small notes, for which gold will be paid, will continue to increase so far as the treasury department is advised. No gold has been engaged at the New York sub-treasury for shipment tomorrow.

Several other offers of gold for small treasury notes were made to the Secretary of the Treasury this afternoon. Cincinnati bankers offer $1,000,000, of which $500,900 was accepted. Other offers in small gum titles come from bankers in Kentucky, Illinois and Missouri. Treasurer Nebeker was much pleased with the turn affairs had taken and declared that sufficient offers of gold had been received to absorb all the small legal tender notes on hand.

CLEVELAND GRATIFIED.

President Cleveland and the cabinet were relieved and gratified by the report which Secretary Carlisle was able to make at the cabinet meeting to-day as to the treasury situation, which indicated to them that there would be no immediate necessity of at large gold reserve. Secretary Carlisle was able to report first, that Assistant Treasurer Roberts of New York had telegraphed to-day that he did not expect any requests from the sub-treasury for gold for export during the next week, and second, that gold was coming into the treasury instead of going out. Of course Secretary Carlisle was enabled to make the latter statement by the offers made by the banks, especially in the west, such as the one of $5,000,000 received from Cincinnati and accepted by him to-day on the plan adopted at Denver of exchanging small notes for it and leaving the gold in the depository banks. He expects to have $50,900,900 of free gold within the next ten days, and is disposed to believe that the tide has now turned in favor of the treasury so that the free gold will increase rather than decrease.

Secretary Carlisle's statement confirmed the President in his belief that the New York bankers who want a new issue of bonds have been endeavoring to force the administration to make one and it is his purpose not to do so unless the conditions change. There is no difference of opinion in the cabinet as to the power of the secretary either to issue bonds or to use a portion of the $50,900,600 reserve. But there is no expectation that either course will be taken.

The cash balance in the treasury shows a slight improvement, as well as the gold balance. The latest declared balance is $25,220,500, of which $11,454,679 is on deposit in national banks, $11,051,189 is in subsidiary silver and $2,714,632 in minor coin and fractional paper.

BOSTON, Jan. 9.—Mrs. William L. Judkins, who occupied with her newborn and seven months old son suite 20 in the Greeley, a family hotel, Hammond street, Roxbury, this afternoon killed her child and then attempted to take her own life. There seems no doubt that she was insane.

Special To the Register.

day has brought to light nothing of interest
bearing on the Senatorial situation, beyond
a few reports which at best are mere
rumors. It has been observed as day of
rest and a Sabbath quiet prevails about
the headquarters of the candidates, and
the lobbies of the hotels. But it is the
calm which precedes the storm. To-mor-
row the forces will again be actively at
work, and as the time for the caucus ap-
proaches there will be some shrewd ma-
nipulation of the political machinery bear-
ing upon the Senatorial contest.

As a matter of fact, the date of the cau-
cus has not yet been determined upon, and
as many friends of all candidates express a
willingness to go into such meeting at
any time, it is quite probable that the
date will be selected by a conference of
leaders on all sides.

A report which is being freely circulat-
ed, and for the authenticity of which your
correspondent does not vouch, is to the eff-
ect that the Camden men are favorable to
the candidacy of Congressman

W. L. WILSON FOR THE UNEXPIRED TERM
made vacant by the death of Senator Ken-
na, and that they will make an effort to
dispose of the short term before going into
caucus for the long term. The re-
port says that the Camden strength

which with the personal following he will
receive from the other side, will be sufi-
cient to bring about his nomination. The
story bears upon its face the marks of
plausibility, but friends of Mr. Wilson as-
sert he would not consent to be a party to
such a course. It is conceded that Mr.
Wilson's election to the unexpired term
would make it difficult to elect Senator
Faulkner to the full term, as the two gen-
tlemen live in adjoining counties and geo-
graphical location sometimes plays an im-
portant part in politics.

Leaving the discussion of possibilities,
probabilities and rumors there are some
facts in connection with the situation which
make interesting reading. It is now gen-
erally conceded that there are but two can-
didates for the full term, Camden and
Faulkner, the other gentlemen mentioned
having withdrawn from the race to enter
the fight for the unexpired term where
they will have a brighter chance of success.
None of the names of men mentioned who
were aspirants for Senatorial honors were
confident of success. Mr. Brockunier's
candidacy will depend largely upon future
developments.

AN INTERESTING MATTER

bearing upon the situation is being dis-
cussed to-day. It is as to the duty of the
Legislature in the event of the receipt of
communication tomorrow from Governor
Fleming, officially announcing the death of
Senator Kenna. Many hold to the opinion
that the Legislature is required by statute
to immediately commence voting for
his successor. Delegate Wm. Z. Lively
made an exhaustive research of the au-
thorities upon the matter, and tonight in-
formed your correspondent that he was
unable to find a line touching upon the
point involved. He gave it as his opinion

cus and the order which the Senators

There seems no end to the discussion of the silver question. Some points in discussion are worthy of more consideration than has been given them.

One, the withdrawal of all bills issued by the government and national banks below the denomination of $10. That would put into circulation many millions of silver coin. It would be received by all of the agricultural and mechanical interests of the country with joy. Once in their possession, much of it would be hoarded, whereas, with United States or bank notes, they are so liable to destruction in so many ways that they are seldom put aside by the people. There is no objection by the masses in the country to silver; the objection comes mainly from the wealthy and the banks. The wealthy man thinks he is overloaded if he has $5 in silver in his pocket. No, he prefers to have it in bank notes. The banks object to silver, because of its bulk; in their business it would require a little more clerical help to handle, and little more vault room to store. Well, certainly, the banks could well afford these increased labors, considering their annual profits and the soundness of their holdings, and it might result to their profit by increasing the sale of exchange. I repeat the main objection to the use of silver coin lays in those two objections. The government should give it its credit, and make it legal tender in any sum, the same as gold, and, like gold to a great extent. It would remain in the vaults of the banks of the nation as basis for credit. The value of gold and silver coin is determined by national legislation; even copper and nickel are made to have a currency value by legislation. The prevalent idea that the purchase of silver bullion by this country is the cause of the withdrawal of gold for export is a mistake.

In your issue of the 14th inst. is reported conversation with Secretary Carlisle, in which he is made to say that the amount of silver bullion purchased during certain period was $49,961,100, and paid for in treasury notes, and that during the same time $47,715,900 was paid in gold for the redemption of said notes. Suppose there had been no silver certificates issued. Could shippers not have presented the United States treasury notes for redemption? Has there never been gold shipped before this year? Why, then, say the notes issued for the purchase of silver bullion was the cause of the withdrawal of gold? The shippers of gold are not bullion sellers, and so long as the government pays out gold for silver certificates, which are redeemable at the option of the government in either gold or silver, they will prefer the gold.

The solution of that question depends wholly upon the balance of trade between this and foreign countries. Look at the balance of trade against us in the past nine months $70,000,000 and if I am not mistaken, about this amount has been drawn from us in gold. Witness the report some two weeks since that large sum in gold would be shipped by next steamer, but there sprung up a demand for cotton and other staples, and furnished the market with bills of exchange, which were taken in preference to gold.

The remedy, therefore, seems to lay in an increase of our exports, or an increase of foreign trade. The purchase of silver bullion has nothing whatever to do with the export of gold. Let the government establish a basis of value for silver equal with that before the Sherman demonetizing act of 1873 was passed, and make it a legal tender for all amounts, and then four-fifths of the people of this country will have cause for rejoicing.

It was called up by Mr. Cotton of Allegheny, who had introduced it amid a storm of noes. Mr. Cotton, however, made humorous speech in its favor, in which he declared it was an important measure. He feared gentlemen of the house did not fully appreciate it or understand its import. He had paid considerable attention to other gentlemen's bills during the session, and he hoped they would give the same consideration to this bill in which he was interested.

Mr. Crawford reminded Mr. Cotton that if the bill passed he would recognize its importance more fully in himself. Mr. Cotton moved to postpone for the present, but the house declined and Mr. Boyer called the yeas and nays on the passage of the resolution. To the surprise of many it carried by vote of 60 to 81.

The Legislature will adjourn Thursday, June 1. A resolution to that effect was adopted Tuesday morning by the Rules Committee, and Mr. Boyer was instructed to report it to the House and the House adopted it.

The House passed finally the following bills: Prohibiting persons, by sale, gift or otherwise, from furnishing cigarettes, containing tobacco or cigarette papers, to minors and providing for the punishment of the same; securing to mechanics, journeymen and laborers the right to liens against real estate for the amount of wages due for work or labor done in and about the construction, alteration or repairing thereof.

The House then proceeded to the consideration on third reading of the Niles double tax bill. Mr. North, of McKean, was the first speaker on the bill. He was opposed to it and gave at great length his reasons. Mr. Branson, of Chester, opposed the bill from a farmers standpoint, and urged the State Tax conference had made its report before passing measure of this kind.

Taggart, of Montgomery, said he did not care whether the manufacturers of his county were for or against the bill. He was for it and said this was the law that he wanted. He claimed they understood it as well as any corporation lawyer on the floor of the House. Martin of Lawrence, and Porter, of Westmoreland spoke in favor of the bill. A vote was then taken on the bill on final passage with the following result: For 60, against 120. Messrs Douthett and Mates voted for the bill.

The senate passed the Free Text Book bill that morning on third reading and it now goes to the governor. The bill received large vote, much to the surprise of its opponents and friends alike. Ross of Bucks, and Mitchell of Bradford, were for it.

The bill provides that the books now in the hands of the pupils shall not be discarded for new books, which will prevent extravagance. The measure embodies the Philadelphia system, which has been in practice for years, and which is commended by educators throughout the country. The measure is to be followed with an appropriation of $500,000, which will be in addition to the $100,000 to the public schools the next ten years. The bill is unquestionably one of the most important that has passed this legislature.

Governor Pattison sent two vetoes to the house Wednesday. One of these was of the bill authorizing the sheriff of Philadelphia to advertise sales in three daily papers.

exact account. In proposing to prolong

political pack in its hands, about to
give away the game that was inevitably
its own2

whether their proposed " compromise"
is better than nothing at all, whether
half loaf is better than no bread, but
whether the party will do what it
promised the people of the United

give them the whole loaf to which it is
pledged and which it is able to give.

that pledge, and it will not do, when
it appears in the next campaign before
the people to give an account Of its
stewardship, to offer the stone of COM
promise for the bread that was solemnly
promised. The people will not accept
compromise in place Of the absolute
performance to which the honor and
faith of the party were plighted. To
substitute one cowardly makeshift'
for another will neither deceive the
country nor relieve the financial
stringency and alarm.

the battle has been sham one in the

true or not, there can be no doubt thai
there is growing suspicion to that
effect, that the country is beginning
to wonder what influences are al
work behind the veil Of senatorial
courtesy" to produce these results
These doubts cannot but be strengthen
ed when we see such compromise as

been brought to the front within the

possible that this compromise is the
result of an effort on the part OF
ambitious rivals to head him off and
to prevent his securing the glory that
might otherwise be his? Stranger
things than this have happened in
politics.

party faith is dearer than shifty devices
